name: Khmeric
region: Cambodia, and Khmer-speaking areas of northeast Thailand and southern Vietnam
defining_innovation: Khmer, the national language of Cambodia, with inscriptions from 611 CE, the longest written record of any Austroasiatic language.

chapters.title: Old Khmer and Angkor
chapters.body: Khmer is written in inscriptions from the 7th century. The earliest dated one, from Angkor Borei, is from 611 CE. Its script developed from southern Indian writing, and the early inscriptions often pair Sanskrit verses with Khmer prose recording donations to temples, lists of land, rice and slaves. Under the Angkor empire (9th–15th centuries) Khmer was the language of a state that dominated mainland Southeast Asia. The Thai and Lao took over much Khmer vocabulary, especially for royalty, government and religion, as well as the Khmer-derived scripts.

chapters.title: Two Registers
chapters.body: Between Old and Modern Khmer, the old voiced consonants lost their voicing and merged with the voiceless ones. The distinction did not vanish: it moved into the vowels, which developed two 'registers'. Syllables that once began with a voiced consonant have a breathier, lower quality and different vowels. The Khmer script still writes the old consonant distinction, and readers use it to choose the vowel. Several neighbouring Austroasiatic languages, Mon among them, went through similar changes.

chapters.title: Modern Khmer
chapters.body: Under the French protectorate (1863–1953), the Buddhist monk and scholar **Chuon Nath** compiled the first great dictionary of Khmer (published from 1938) and coined Khmer and Pali-based words for modern concepts. This laid the foundation of the standard language. Under the Khmer Rouge (1975–1979) teachers, monks and writers were killed in large numbers, and much of the country's literature and many of its books were destroyed.

speakers.note: Khmer is the national language of Cambodia; Northern Khmer in Thailand is under pressure from Thai and Lao.

turning_points.title: The first dated Khmer inscription
turning_points.description: An inscription from Angkor Borei is the earliest dated text in Khmer, written in a script of southern Indian origin, alongside Sanskrit. Hundreds of Old Khmer inscriptions follow.

sources.citation: Jenny, Mathias & Paul Sidwell, eds. 2015. The Handbook of Austroasiatic Languages. Leiden: Brill.

turning_points.title: Angkor and its neighbours
turning_points.description: Sanskrit and Pali vocabulary flows into Khmer, and Khmer in turn gives Thai and Lao much of their royal, administrative and religious vocabulary, along with their scripts.

sources.citation: Jenny, Mathias & Paul Sidwell, eds. 2015. The Handbook of Austroasiatic Languages. Leiden: Brill.

turning_points.title: Voicing becomes register
turning_points.description: Voiced stops merge with voiceless ones, and the lost contrast survives as two vowel registers, with the old voiced series giving a breathier, lower-register vowel. Khmer spelling still reflects the old consonants.
turning_points.notation: *b *d *ɡ → p t k, with the old voicing kept as a breathy second register on the vowel

sources.citation: Jenny, Mathias & Paul Sidwell, eds. 2015. The Handbook of Austroasiatic Languages. Leiden: Brill.

turning_points.title: Chuon Nath's dictionary
turning_points.description: Chuon Nath's Khmer dictionary and his new Khmer and Pali-based coinages give Cambodia a modern standard language that is less dependent on French.

sources.citation: Jenny, Mathias & Paul Sidwell, eds. 2015. The Handbook of Austroasiatic Languages. Leiden: Brill.
